actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species is distributed circumglobally in tropical and subtropical seas. In the Indo-Pacific it is known from the Red Sea, along East Africa to South Africa (Tsitsikamma Coastal National Park), Madagascar, India, Sri Lanka, and all major island groups, the Seychelles, Australia (Elizabeth and Middleton Reefs, Lord Howe Island, and northern New South Wales (29°S) to Rowley Shoals), Mascarenes, New Caledonia and Kermadecs to Rotuma, Pitcairn Island, southern Japan, and the Hawaiian Islands. It does not occur in the Persian Gulf (D. Feary pers. comm. 2014). In the eastern Pacific it is known from Mexico to Chile. In the western Atlantic it is known from Massachusetts south along the U.S., Bermuda, the Bahamas, throughout the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea, and along South America to Bahia State (Brazil) including Trinidade Island (Simon et al. 2013). In the eastern Atlantic it is known from Ascension, St Helena, and Fernando Po.
documentation.population:
This species appears to be common, but not abundant. It occurs at a low density (<0.01 ind/m²) in Culebra Bay, Gulf of Papagayo, Costa Rica (Dominici-Arosemena et al. 2005). It is rare in the Bismarck Sea based on 2006 survey (Hamilton et al. 2009). It is also rare off northwest Madagascar (McKeena and Allen 2005), in Milne Bay Province, Papua New Guinea (Allen et al. 2003), in the Gulf of Thailand (Scaps 2006), at Cape Panwa reef site, Phuket, Thailand (Satapoomin 1999), and in American Samoa (Fishes of National Park of American Samoa).

Diodon hystrix is considered one of the three major species of puffer fishes on the coast of India. Total estimated pufferfish stock size off the Lakshaweep Islands (major reef of India) was 74,974 individuals in 2008. Of this stock, a maximum yield was estimated as 50,783 individuals (Gopakumar 2008).

The species is rare off Fort Lauderdale, Florida (Jordan et al. 2005) and in Looe Key National Marine Sanctuary, Florida (Bohnsack et al. 1987). It had a percent frequency (% sighting frequency) of 13% and density score of 1.1 in Cayman Island based on expert sightings from 1994-2001 (Pattengil-Semmens and Semmens 2003).
documentation.habitats: Diodon hystrix is a reef-associated species occurring in subtropical waters to depths between 2 and 50 m, but is usually found between 3 and 20 m (Gasparini and Floeter 2001, Leis 2001, Florida Museum of Natural History 2005). Adults are benthic and commonly seen in caves and holes in shallow reefs (Sommer et al. 1996, Smith 1997, Kuiter and Tonozuka 2001). Juveniles can be found in mangrove habitats off the Yucatan coast (Mexico) (M. Vega-Cendejas pers. comm. 2015) and Pacific Panama (R. Robertson pers. comm. 2015). Its diet consists of sea urchins, gastropods, and hermit crabs (Leis 2001). Maximum total length is 91 cm (Eschmeyer et al. 1983); it commonly reaches a total length of 40 cm (Sanches 1991); maximum published weight is 2.8 kg (IGFA 2001).
documentation.threats: There are no major threats known for this species.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for this fish.
documentation.use_trade: This species is dried and sold as curios in parts of its range. It is eaten in Hawaii and Tahiti (Leis 1978). There are reports that it is toxic to humans, however this needs to be substantiated. It occurs in the aquarium trade through Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil; between 1995 to 2000, 896 individuals were traded, which constitutes about 0.45% of all the marine ornamental fish trade (Monteiro-Neto et al. 2003). A total of 2,050 individuals of this species has been caught in Hawaii from 1967-2003. It is regularly observed in fish markets in Samporna, Malaysia (B. Stockwell pers. comm. 2011).
documentation.rationale: This species is widely distributed and occurs on shallow coral or rocky reefs. There are no known major threats, therefore it is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Diodon hystrix has a very wide distribution and a genetic analysis is warranted.
